#4050. Smash hit cyberpunk storekeeper Probably Stolen was originally a different, non-cyberpunk game that seemed destined to sink without trace

Publisher tinyBuild celebrates turnaround after very underwhelming demo numbers

Space station trading game Probably Stolen – Cyberpunk Shopkeeper Sim has been doing rather well on Steam, attracting over 162,000 concurrent players last night. I've been feeling the urge to fire it up again myself, after my brief launch-day trawl through its quagmire of black market economics and factional rivalries.

The game's big numbers come as a shock given that it began life as another, non-cyberpunk kiosk job sim called Deepspace Emporium, which still has a Steam page as of writing. Deepspace Emporium seemed doomed to fizzle out in obscurity. But publisher tinyBuild got behind it regardless, working with developers Questing Goose to overhaul the art direction and lay on extra brainchips. The gamble paid off.

"Probably Stolen was initially a game under a different name with a released demo," summarises tinyBuild CEO Alex Nichiporchik on Twitter. "That demo peaked at 28 concurrent players. We loved the concept and gameplay, and worked with the dev to reinvent the visuals and focus on what works design wise. This is the result."

The original Deepspace Emporium seems very similar to Probably Stolen in broad strokes. The core of the game is haggling with strung-out ne'er-do-wells, buying or selling goods of varying quality and legality in order to surf a fluctuating market and pay the rent. It's Papers, Please, but you're searching for fake watermarks on cigarette packets, and wondering whether you dare stock contraband weaponry. You also have to appease or outmanouevre factions with competing interests, from station security to underworld barons.

From what I've played, Probably Stolen essentially takes all that and pumps up the Netrunner parallels with posher visuals. Not having played the now-unavailable Deepspace demo, I can't say how much intrigue it adds to all the shady transactions going on beneath the hood.

I'm not blown away by Probably Stolen's pixelart – I find it quite flavourless, as depictions of cyberpunk space stations go – but it has pleasing texture. I am disproportionately fond of the rolled-up sleeping mat beneath my counter. Looks nicely padded! Still, the meat of this game is undoubtedly the vast collection of items you can get your greasy fingers on, with a choice of retail lines and vocational pathways such as gunsmith and chemist. You can sell rat corpses, tins of caviar, robotic hands, scavenged shotguns, and purple tubers of uncertain origin. I am Commander Silverhand, and this is my favourite store on the Citadel.

It's lovely to think of a developer transforming a probable write-off into a chart-topper by means of some canny plumping and reorganising. The situation is almost certainly more complicated than Nichiporchik makes it sound. Still, let's take the opportunity to reminisce moist-eyed about a few other games that underwent a dramatic visual transformation during development.

The obvious one is Team Fortress 2, which once upon a time looked like a prototype Silent Hill environment with some khaki toy soldiers. Gearbox worked similar sorcery upon Borderlands, which once looked like a hungover Fallout 3. The prevailing wisdom is that piping in some colour and whimsy propelled these games to greatness, but who knows, perhaps if they'd clung to the old "football stadium toilet bowl" vibe, they'd have made an extra billion apiece. Any other precedents come to your mind?

#4049. Crimson Desert's first patch aims at fixing controls, but it mostly affects mouse and keyboard

The first post-launch patch for Crimson Desert is here, and the list of changes is promising, even if it doesn't go far enough to address some deeper issues.

Crimson Desert has been out for a few days now, and as positive as its been received by many players, the game suffers from several fundamental issues that anyone who’s played it has called out.

Perhaps the loudest one of those has been how the game controls, which is a problem that stems from the complexity of controls themselves, as well as the underlying animations behind many of the actions the player character performs.

In the first case, at least, something is being done.

Developer Pearl Abyss rolled out patch 1.00.03 for Crimson Desert on Monday. The patch is available now on Steam and PlayStation, with Xbox and the Epic Games Store following “at a later time.”

Today’s update follows a letter to players the developer issued on Saturday. The letter generally acknowledged player feedback, but specifically pointed to complaints about the game’s clunky controls as something of a focus for the team.

The action RPG has actually broken its launch peak concurrent player numbers over the weekend, though only by a few thousands more. Its Steam user review rating has also improved over the same period.

This latest update only includes an initial set of fixes, but Pearl Abyss vowed to keep working on addressing all other points of feedback. A highlight in 1.00.03 is the addition of a Storage at Howling Hill Camp, which can be used to store inventory items.

The most important changes, of course, affect how the game controls on keyboard and mouse. Pearl Abyss included several fixes and altered some of the default presets to make the experience less painful when playing the game with a keyboard and mouse.

There are sadly no changes to controllers, but it is something that the developer said we can expect to see in future patches. More improvements for keyboard and mouse setups are in the works, too.

Beyond the control changes, patch 1.00.03 also includes a set of gameplay tweaks, especially when it comes to enemy health and difficulty. It also makes fast travelling more convenient, and brings a few fixes to NPC dialogue. You can read the full change log on Steam.

#4047. Stalker 2’s first expansion officially revealed, and it's taking us to the power plant where it all began

Stalker 2’s first add-on isn’t far off, and it may just be the thing to bring you back to post-apocalyptic Chornobyl in 2026.

One of the biggest reveals out of today’s Xbox Partner Preview showcase has been the new Stalker 2 expansion. The developer did tease some sort of announcement ahead of the event, but I don’t think an expansion was on many of our bingo cards.

Cost of Hope is the big news; a new add-on that the developer has wisely decided to reveal fairly close to release. Or, at least, the planned release target.

First off, Cost of Hope is set for release this summer. It’ll arrive on all current platforms simultaneously, meaning PC, Xbox, and PlayStation. The expansion is described as “non-linear”, and it takes place in the heartlands, deeper into the Zone.

The story revolves around a conflict between Duty, and Freedom, two factions whose idea of the what the Zone is and their understanding of its possibilities differ widely. You’ll be playing as protagonist Skif once again, and the expansion’s events will run parallel to the main game.

GSC Game World says Cost of Hope will introduce two new regions, offering dozens of hours of gameplay. We’ll get to actually explore the Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant as part of the expansion, alongside the Iron Forest.

Each of the two new regions will have its own hub area, NPCs, quests, activities and stories. Of course, it wouldn’t be a Stalker expansion without some new weapons, and Cost of Hope promises a few - some can even be seen in the trailer.

The developer also confirmed that there’s one other story DLC in the works. Together with Heart of Chornobyl, and Cost of Hope all three will form a trilogy of interconnected stories. More details on Cost of Hope - including a release date - will be revealed sometime in the summer.

#4046. "The Series Was In Dire Straits" - Kit & Krysta Recall Zelda's Pre-BOTW Dark Times

While many of us can now look back on the Skyward Swords of the Zelda series with fondness, those who were in the trenches at the time might recall that things were starting to feel stagnant.

The later games of the 'traditional' Zelda formula were well received critically, but the tried-and-tested gameplay wasn't working wonders for their sales numbers, and they were struggling to bring in new fans in the process.

Cue the open-world series reinvention in Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom.

With Ocarina of Time back in the public eye (perhaps the most typical 'Zelda' a Zelda game can get), there are some who are wondering why it has been so long since we've seen the traditional format. So, naturally, former Nintendo employees Kit & Krysta are on hand to remind us all just how dark things were getting before the invigorating shot of BOTW.

"There has been some revisionist history out there lately about how the Zelda team 'ripped these [traditional format games] away from us at the peak of their popularity'," Kit Ellis said on the latest episode of the duo's podcast before setting the record straight.

"The series was in, like, dire straits," Krysta Yang added, "it was selling like nothing". Kit recalls going to focus groups and receiving feedback like, "the fanbase is dwindling; this is not bringing in new players; the interest is getting smaller".

With the huge success of Zelda today, it's easy to forget that such a time ever existed — particularly for those who weren't all that deep on the series at the time.

"It was depressing," Krysta adds, "it was like, we are losing this."

Of course, Breath of the Wild was so immensely popular and so very unlike anything we had seen from the series before that it gave Zelda the interest boost it so desperately needed. It's interesting to see how well-received the return of the classic format has been with OoT, so perhaps we'll see something slightly more traditional make an appearance in the next mainline game.

The dream scenario would be Nintendo leaving room for both formats to develop, but it's far too early to know what the team is cooking up for the next mainline entry. Until then, we have the pinnacle of the open-world structure and the very best of the traditional at our fingertips on Switch 2, so we're more than happy to wait and see what comes next.

News It's Official, Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Has Sold Over 5 Million Copies In 4 Days

In June 2011, Ocarina 3D came out and sold pretty well. The it had given the 3DS another boom in units sold, but it didn’t last the whole Summer, resulting in a dramatic price drop for the system a couple months in, to make it cheaper than even the price which the DSi launched at.

Both Donkey Kong Country Returns and Super Mario Galaxy 2 sold more than twice that amount. In the 2011 holiday season, Mario Kart Wii and New Super Mario Bros. Wii sold more, despite releasing in 2008 and 2011 respectively.

There was still certainly more hype and excitement than most games on the market. The big thing it was competing up against however was Skyrim, that just had universal praise and a virality like no other game at that time.

But, it was also a pretty late Wii game. Nintendo focused their efforts onto 3DS, which had made Skyward Sword a bit of a 2011 straggler. In that year, both Xbox and Playstation gained ground as incredible games were releasing then, alongside some more advanced motion-sensing technology to draw noise. The Wii was older news and had Skyward Sword released in 2010, like it was originally supposed to, I think you get a much different conversation about the popularity of that game. But, this sort of competition of Zelda getting slightly snubbed happens regularly too. Baldur’s Gate 3 narrowly sold more than Tears of the Kingdom, and snatched more awards too.

Regardless, in the 2013 Wii U Direct, Nintendo made it a point to say that the the next Zelda title after Skyward Sword would have its linear structure entirely challenged and go back to basics.

Before we even knew Breath of the Wild’s title, story, or aesthetic, Nintendo wanted to tell us that the structure would change and make it their selling point. You really only make that remark when you sense from your fans that they are ready for a change.

So, I do think that was because the series was viewed at as something very conservative in its approach and Nintendo caught on to that. The formula of a Zelda game was well understood and Skyward Sword did little to change that. Comparatively, A Link Between Worlds was looked at as something with a middleground between fresh and historied, being the sequel to the the game that would establish the “Zelda formula.” I don’t think it was in “dire straights,” to the extent that it was threatened as not being one of Nintendo’s most important franchises, but it was considered to be predicatable in its approach, and maybe even a little tired.

I really hate when people blame the level design for Skyward Sword's commercial struggles. The Wii was all but abandoned by the time the game launched while Xbox was in its golden age with the 360 and Sony was firing on all cylinders playing catch-up after PS3's slow start. Wii was barely getting any AAA first or third party games and had developed a reputation as a "casual" console, taking the brunt of the motion control fatigue that set in after both their competitors jumped on that bandwagon and helped run it into the ground. I'll admit that open worlds still being a novelty back then and Skyrim launching around the same time didn't do it any favors, but I'm also baffled by Fromsoft getting all the credit for the subsequent wave of "souls-likes" when those games' level designs feel so obviously inspired by Zelda.

I saw a lot of the trend/demand dying for Zelda when I worked at gamestop. The series has its diehard fans, but it wasn’t pulling in new interest. The stories were considered too lighthearted/childish by many mainstream consumers. They wanted adventure that was gritty, often bloody and less magical. Also less talkative (a complaint I will never understand about RPGS or adventure games) JRPGs were also hitting a downward tilt/over saturation and some of that is still a thing. People eat up soulsbore games for their bleak, difficult worlds and while the lore is dense…the player has to look for it (and half of that is inferred). While kids wanted shooters and ballers.

Nintendo tried to keep the formula fresh with control schemes and art styles but they weren’t seeing consistent returns. The Zelda cycle is/was a real thing as you’d watch a Zelda game get rave reviews but not the sales numbers to match or later become a misunderstood classic (WW,MM,SS,PH). BOTW changed that by essentially going back to Zelda’s roots. Here’s a big arse map, gather stuff to beat Gannon, good luck. The first Zelda game let you tackle the first 8 dungeons for the most part however you wanted (how hard that was or how many times you died was a different story) BOTW brought that back (and was less strict even as you don’t have to do the main story really to beat ganon). BOTW was also a launch/gen straddle game. I do think there is a natural surge in potential consumers as many fans are now middle aged and introduced their kids to the franchise.

I’m just glad Nintendo is stubborn about certain franchises. Which I suspect is more due to the producers in charge that believe in the franchise than anything. Nintendo has employees that either spent their lives working on these franchises or grew up with them. So it is still a product but there is almost a heritage aspect to it that many companies don’t have.

I am a lifelong fan of the Zelda series and grew up right alongside it. The original came out when I was 7 years old, and I've owned and played them all ever since. I think I can generally agree with what Kit and Krista are saying, from a fan's perspective at that time (mid 2010s).

I never finished Skyward Sword, the first mainline title that I didn't like. I really disliked the control scheme and character design, and the game structure just left me frustrated and bored.

I had similar feelings for Phantom Hourglass and Spirit Tracks, which were earlier but both forced in too much of those pesky touch controls I didn't like.

I genuinely thought the series was saved by the 3DS. I adored Ocarina of time 3D, which replaced the original as my all-time favorite game in any series or platform. A Link Between Worlds was fantastic. Majora's Mask 3D completely changed how I feel about that game, for the better.

Then Tri Force Heroes came along and I once again had a Zelda game that left me cold.

Breath of the Wild saved the series for me and remains my favorite game I've ever played. I have hundreds and hundreds of hours in it. I won't spend nearly as much time with the new Ocarina of Time, but it's arguably a more polished and refined title. I'm very happy with what Nintendo has done for Zelda since 2017.

#4045. Lucky Luke Retro Collection Brings Several Games to the US for the Very First Time

Atari has announced another retro games collection, and this one marks the United States debut of multiple old school classics.

This is Lucky Luke: The Lonesome Cowboy Collection, a compilation of retro titles developed by Graphite Lab and published by Infogrames. It's scheduled for launch on PS5 and PS4 on 13th January, 2027.

For those that don't know, Lucky Luke is a character that's been around since the 1940s. Originally a French-Belgian comic book character, he predates Asterix and The Smurfs, and has been adapted across various media throughout the decades.

That includes video games, of course, and six of his previous interactive excursions are included here:

"Every game features quality-of-life improvements, including improved graphics, save states, achievements, visual filters, custom screen bezels, and rebindable controls," reads the press release. "'How to Play' guides onboard unfamiliar players and help them solve difficult challenges."

Interestingly, several of these games never made it outside of Europe; in the above list, I've put an asterisk next to the games that will be brought to the USA for the first time in this collection.

As well as just compiling classic titles, the Lonesome Cowboy Collection includes a bonus called the Frontier Experience, which is a brand new, first-person feature that acts as a museum mode and shooting gallery.

You can use this mode to learn more about each game, hunt down collectibles, play minigames, and view old artwork.

I remember playing a demo of Lucky Luke on the PS1 back in the day, and can still recall the music from that one stage I went through over and over again.

Are you interested in Lucky Luke: The Lonesome Cowboy Collection? Tell us in the comments section below.

Stephen has been part of the Push Square team for over six years, bringing boundless enthusiasm and a deep knowledge of video games to his role as Assistant Editor. Having grown up playing every PlayStation console to date, he's developed an eclectic taste, with particular passion for indie games, arcade racers, and puzzlers. He's also our go-to guy for Sonic-related matters, much to his delight/chagrin.

#4044. Asha Sharma Issues Statement On Xbox's 25th Anniversary And The Future Of Gaming

"Our largest studios will be able to pursue ambitions as far beyond today’s games"

We've been waiting all week for Xbox to acknowledge its 25th anniversary in a formal fashion, and Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has now issued a statement discussing the past, present and future of the brand to celebrate its birthday.

It's a pretty lengthy statement, and a lot of it is just about recapping the history of Xbox and Microsoft Gaming as a whole. Sharma talks about how things have come a long way since "Microsoft Adventure" in 1979, and then how Xbox was "impossible to miss" in 2001 while also revolutionising online play and being there for the launch of Halo.

There's also a cool high-definition ad for the original Xbox console that you can see down below.

"When the original XBOX launched in 2001, it was impossible to miss. It was 2-3x larger than rival consoles, with a giant X molded into a black enclosure and a bright alien green jewel at the center..."

"A year later, Xbox Live revolutionized online play with persistent friend lists and matchmaking, as well as a common service for developers to build connected experiences. And bringing all of this together was Halo: Combat Evolved, a launch title that not only defined XBOX but proved its first advertising campaign: “Games Will Never Be The Same.”

After going through the history, Sharma mentions that each of the 111 people who have worked at Xbox since the beginning will be getting "a special engraved console to commemorate what you’ve helped build".

She then references the fans, Xbox FanFest and how today's FanFest event in Seattle will "bring the celebration home".

"The story of XBOX has never been ours alone. Our fans have challenged us, cheered us on, held us accountable, and stuck with us. We’ve been celebrating this anniversary with fans around the world and special launches. Today, we are bringing the celebration home to Seattle."

And finally, the most notable bit in this statement is probably what she says about the "next 25" years of Xbox, highlighting that the "cost, resources, and risk required" to create modern games has grown dramatically, and that it's had an impact on the ability to turn ideas into games, or at least allow those ideas to reach their potential.

As a result, she says it's something that "must" be changed, and that people and small teams will "soon" be able to achieve things that currently require much larger teams and financial resources in today's world.

"While modern games demonstrate the heights of human craft in ways unimaginable just decades ago, the cost, resources, and risk required to create them have grown just as dramatically. As a result, too many ideas never become games, and too many games fall short of what their creators imagined. For decades, this has been the unavoidable tradeoff of ambition. We must change this."

"Throughout human history, the scale of what we could create was determined by the people, capital, and resources we could command. That relationship is beginning to break. A single person will soon be able to wield capabilities that once required entire nations. A small team will be able to build worlds that today demand hundreds of developers and hundreds of millions of dollars. And our largest studios will be able to pursue ambitions as far beyond today’s games as Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024 is from its first entry in 1982."

"I believe the future of gaming will look more like its beginning, when a small team with a big idea could change how the world plays. Our responsibility is to deliver great games, unmistakable hardware, and give more people the chance to make something the world has never seen."

There's some interesting stuff in here for sure, and we reckon it might be worth keeping an eye on tonight's Seattle Xbox FanFest event for any potential announcements - after all, it's the final stop and "home" destination for the FanFest tour.

For now though, let us know what you think about Asha Sharma's statement down below!

Yes. The passage is strongly AI-related, although it never explicitly mentions artificial intelligence.

It appears to be alluding to the transformative potential of AI, particularly generative AI, in video game development.

1. "A single person will soon be able to wield capabilities that once required entire nations."

2. "A small team will be able to build worlds that today demand hundreds of developers."

3. "The cost, resources, and risk required to create them have grown dramatically."

No. The passage deliberately avoids mentioning AI, machine learning, or generative AI.

The underlying message is that AI and emerging technology will fundamentally change the economics and scale of video game development.

The author is suggesting that the next generation of games will be created with fewer people, fewer resources, and significantly greater creative ambition.

The wording is particularly interesting because it frames AI not simply as a way to cut jobs or costs, but as a way to enable creative possibilities that were previously impossible.

My verdict: I would interpret this as an indirect statement about the future of AI in gaming, with AI likely being a major part of the vision, even though the passage carefully avoids naming it directly.

I'm probably in the minority here, @HonestHick, but I really do not care if a game is made entirely by AI (which it surely will at some point!).

The way I look at it is that AI is just a natural progression of the technological revolution. Just as with the Industrial Revolution, humans will adapt to it happening, and will find other means of employment, and just as with the Industrial Revolution it won't happen all at once, it will be a gradual process of replacing certain tasks within game development, with the dynamic of who does what changing over many years rather than all of a sudden. In a decade, when AI involvement will be much greater, it will be largely accepted that this is the way games get made. Right now, there is resistance within the gaming community, but as time goes on, and AI usage becomes more prevalent, so too will the acceptance of the gaming community that this is the way of things.

I think what will sway things is that games will be made faster; potentially a lot faster. AAA games that take 5 to 7 years to make now, will be made in 2 to 3 years, and then possibly fewer than that as AI improves and is more deeply implemented.

What should also happen, is that games will cost a lot less to be made, and hopefully that will be passed on to the consumer. If a game costs £200 million to be made now, it needs to be sold at £70 in the hope of recouping that money. With AI heavily involved, that development costs far, far less, and I think those companies that pass on those savings to the gaming community may find that it is very much appreciated.

So, if games can be made more quickly, and cost less, then I personally do not see the downsides of that because regardless of AI humans will always be involved somewhere along the process...

First of all, nobody was talking specifically about AI. AI is only one part of the tools that are available today to make game development easier. For years now, development tools and resources have become increasingly accessible to small teams and even to solo developers. Just remember Bright Memory, released in 2019 and developed by a single person using Unreal Engine. Back then, AI wasn't even being discussed the way it is today. Several of these tools are free, including Unreal Engine, and if you're passionate enough, you can develop a game on your own or with a small team without needing a massive budget.

As for AI, yes, of course it speeds up production processes. But that's not a bad thing. In fact, it's mostly a positive when you actually understand the topic. It can also significantly reduce production costs without sacrificing quality when used properly. I use AI every day, and it really depends on how you use it. It all comes down to what tasks you delegate to AI, how you use it, and what you keep as a human-driven creative process, especially when it comes to artistic decisions.

It is a tool, and it will be used as such, and like all tools throughout the history of man, they are used to make our lives easier. Quite how that statement is extremely limited, I'm not sure...

@HonestHick My man of reason. Keep it going!

@Fiendish-Beaver Sorry, I stopped after your first two comments, which implied she was only talking about AI and suggested it wasn't a good thing. I read your other comments afterward and saw that you became more nuanced following other people's replies.

Either way, I still maintain that she was talking about the evolution of the industry in general, the accessibility of development tools, and how easy they are to use for small teams—hence my example of Bright Memory, which was created by a single person in 2019 and without AI (generative AI didn't even exist yet).

Of course she's also implying the use of AI, that goes without saying. Who doesn't see AI taking an even bigger role in video games? It's obvious!

And we agree: when used properly, AI is ultimately a good thing for the consumer (maybe a bit less so for developers handling low-value tasks)—it all depends on how it's used.

@Fiendish-Beaver You are not the only one to think this - it is quite clearly what she is saying - she's just being carefully to not state her vision is AI. We knew this from the moment she was appointed, so there is little suprise. As someone who believes that human creativity is best I'm not particularly happy that they are sacking as many as they are doing and going all in on AI. But as a gamer just looking for good gaming experiences, I'll reserve judgement until I see the games and experience this 'new vision' for myself.

I'm of the same mindset, @Titntin. I won't boycott a good game using AI just because it uses AI. All I really want, at the end of the day, is to enjoy the games I play, and if it is created using AI so be it.

I don't want to sound heartless, and I don't like the idea of passionate developers using their jobs, but throughout history man has developed tools to make their jobs easier, less laborious, faster and ultimately cheaper. People losing their jobs to a new technology has happened ever since the start of the Industrial Revolution began.

Worldwide, as new tools and methods became available, we saw miners replaced by machinery. The same happened in the car industry where robots replaced human workers. In each of those examples (which happened in my lifetime) the workers found alternative employment, and the same will be true of game development; as AI becomes more and more capable, it will become more and more prevalent, and as it does more and more developers will find themselves being replaced (which I think is what Sharma is banking on as she dismisses 3200 employees this year). Many of those developers will move to other studios not yet in a position to deploy AI and still needing the human guiding hand, and some will move to completely different employment.

Ultimately, I think human involvement in gaming will always be a thing, but over the next decade, many of them will be gradually replaced, and we, the gamer, will embrace the good games that come out. If AI is not up to the required standard, then the games will fail, but as time goes on, I can foresee that many of the games we play will have had heavy input from AI, and providing they are good, we will simply play what we are offered, and our protestations regarding the use of AI will gradually peter out just as happened with all the strikes when the car industry was changing, for example, and we will accept that change is inevitable because like it or not change is coming...

#4043. "Keep talking about it": Raw Power Games call for Wishlist aid as they, and their historical strategy sandbox Chronicles: Medieval, lose funding

Raw Power Games, an independent studio comprising veteran developers of The Witcher 3, Total War: Three Kingdoms, and Crusader Kings III (among others), have called on players for support after losing their funding - an existential threat to both the organisation and to their debut, the still-in-development historical strategy game Chronicles: Medieval.

In a statement posted last week, Raw Power announced that "the necessary funding" behind the studio was no longer in place, despite Chronicles: Medieval – which was unveiled last year with an expensive-looking, Tom Hardy-narrated trailer – apparently being within touching distance of its planned early access launch. Hardy or no Hardy, however, the statement declared that they aren't "going down without a fight", hinting at talks with what could be possible new investors, asking interested would-be fans to "keep talking about" the game, and encouraging its inclusion on Steam Wishlists.

A few days on, the impact of this rallying call remains unclear. Raw Power Games have made no further statements, and Chronicles: Medieval does not seem to appear on Steam's own list of Top Wishlisted games. SteamDB have it at #26 in their desire-o-rankings, representing no change from its position immediately before the funding announcement was made, and while the game's Steam follower count has increased by over 1,000 week-on-week – significantly more so than surrounding games in the list – that doesn't feel like the kind of wild grassroots support that might save a dozens-strong studio.

Still, as my childhood television used to say, every little helps, and I'm inclined to hope for Raw Power's survival if only as an antidote to the enthusiasm-poisining dread of seeing so many other developers being laid off and shut down. Chronicles: Medieval looks promisingly ambitious too, mashing up sprawling Mount & Blade-style battles with an RPG-flavoured strategy layer that involves the player's custom-created character ascending the snooty social hierarchy of 14th century England. Best of luck to everyone trying to get it over the early access line.

#4042. Never one to lag behind HSR and ZZZ, Genshin Impact will introduce its own new pink-haired animal-themed girl in Version Luna 6

Plus Mondstadt is expanding yet further north in Genshin Impact's Luna 6 update.

Today’s Genshin Impact Special Program has wrapped up, and it’s brought us some big news about the next major update. Luna 6 is the next phase in the action RPG’s story, titled Song of the Welkin Moon: Rondo - Augured Homecoming.

It’s set to arrive on April 8, bringing with it a tonne of new content, including a big expansion to the original region of Mondstadt.

As part of this new update, Mondstadt’s northern parts expand with new areas. The new Dornman Port is one thing, but the most exciting is the Temple of Space. This floating structure is home to Asmoday fragments, and is made up of different realms inspired by Liyue, Sumeru, and various other civilizations from around Teyvat. Launching with the update is a new mechanic that lets you manipulate the space to reveal hidden paths containing secrets.

If you take the time to explore, you’ll find a lot to there to learn about Asmoday, Ruler of Space. There’s a new boss to take on in the temple, too: Watcher: Fallen Vigil.

The only new character in Luna 6 is Linnea, who continues the current trend within HoYoverse games of focussing heavily on cute pink-haired animal-themed girls. Linnea is a 5-Star Geo Bow user who can really work with parties made up of Lunar-Crystallize characters, with her big gimmick being the ability to turn Hydro-Crystallize reactions into Lunar-Crystallize reactions.

Linnea has a companion, Lumi, who allows her to increase the Lunar-Crystallize damage she deals, while also lowering her enemies’ Geo resistance. Linnea can also deliver either off-field Geo damage or a Lunar-Crystallize reaction hit with her Elemental Skill.

Beyond that, she can heal the party using her Elemental Burst. If you take Linnea with you as you explore, she can help you discover rare animals, thanks to her innate naturalist abilities.

This update will also see Chasca get her first-ever rerun, and you’ll be able to roll for her in the first phase of Event Wishes. The second phase will feature no new characters and instead focus on Nefer and Lauma. There’s going to be another Chronicled Wish banner, this time specifically for Fontaine characters.

You can look forward to a few other new arrivals in Luna 6, including The Nod-Krai Trade Expo, some quality of life updates to Miliastra Wonderland to up the number of players in each lobby, not to mention various other UI changes.

#4041. Fate of the Galaxy is a huge, fully-featured Star Wars space combat sim that, thanks to being a total conversion mod for Freespace Open, even runs on my rubbish laptop

Star Wars has been back in the news recently because, to cut a long story short, the US alt-right have decided that Darth Vader was actually the good guy. We are not here to indulge such buffoonery. We are here to talk about Fate of the Galaxy, a free unofficial space combat simulator set during the events of the original Star Wars trilogy, featuring several mission-based campaigns and a stable of Imperial and Rebel Alliance ships that ranges from the quad-blasting X-Wing to Boba Fett's Firespray 31. Also, Naboo starfighters, if you really must.

It's a total conversion of poor dead Volition's venerable dogfighter FreeSpace 2, running on the open source Free Space 2 Open engine via the popular Knossos launcher. You don't need a copy of FreeSpace 2 to play it. You also don't need to pay. And nor do you need a whizbang PC – this bucket of bolts hums along happily on my i5-1145G7 with no dedicated graphics card. As the Rancor said to the padawan: finally, some good food.

Fate of the Galaxy has been in development off and on for almost two decades, weathering a number of team changes and shifts of focus. The FreeSpace Wiki has a longer account of its travels. It's not an officially licensed Star Wars production, as made evident by a scrolling text intro which takes the official orchestral theme and moves every note up or down a place, as though spitefully jolting the piano around under John Williams' fingers. It's not quite as bizarre as Portsmouth Sinfonia's Also sprach Zarathustra but it did make me cackle like the Emperor contemplating a freshly made asteroid field. But then I began playing, and my presumptuous merriment became a frown of concentration.

While hardly Steel Battalion, Fate of the Galaxy is a proper nerdy sim with a bustling 3D cockpit and all sorts of keyboard shortcuts to try once and immediately forget. You'll need to funnel energy between fore and aft shields during bombing runs on Star Destroyers, target individual subsystems with your ion cannon, give orders to other pilots, and consider whether to synch different guns for maximum effect. I can run the game fine on my work laptop with integrated graphics, but I'm definitely feeling the need for a beefier keyboard. And also a joystick. Certainly, I'm not going to get far in LAN multiplayer with this hunk of junk.

It seems a very generous production, based on 30 minutes playing kiss-chase with TIE bombers. The story campaigns and quickfix stand-alone skirmishes aside, there's a mission editor with text-based files for easier sharing. There's also VR support with head-tracking, should you own one of those haunted helmets. Learn more via the online manual (Google Doc), and find Fate of the Galaxy itself on Moddb. You'll need around seven gigs of disc space.

This being the year 2026, there's the question of generative AI usage - a topic of much concern lately in modding circles. Fate of the Galaxy's official site boasts that all the visual assets were "made by humans only". I'm less sure about other aspects – there's seemingly some artificial VO during the tutorial, though it sounds like antiquated, less insidious robocaller software. The FreeSpace Open engine itself greatly pre-dates today's chatbot invasion. The original FreeSpace 2 launched in 1999 - a more civilised age, when everybody still thought Darth Vader was an arsehole.

#4040. Caleb's third Myth has finally arrived in Love and Deepspace, and it's good news for all the husbandbro fans out there

Love and Deepspace has kicked off a new event, squarely built around Caleb's new Memory Pair.

Love and Deepspace’s latest update is here, adding a new Memory Pair for Caleb. The event is dubbed Ghosts' Final March, and it’s available now as part of a new Limited Wish Pool, as it has always worked.

The new Memory Pair is a 5-Star Solar-Slot, which can be obtained through the aforementioned Wish Pool. Doing so will unlock the Netherlord Companion for Caleb, and there’s even more for you to explore in this one.

Alongside the big new Memory Pair, Ghosts' Final March also offers the opportunity to earn a new 4-Star Solar-Slot Memory Pair, alongside ten Deepspace Wishes, 500 Diamonds, and other freebies. The event ends on April 11, so you have some time to get in and play.

If you’re only interested in the 5-Star variants, you’ll be happy to know that Infold is sticking with 150 pulls as the absolute maximum to guarantee earning Netherlord. This will be automatically unlocked after you pull both Nether Yearning and Nether Parting through the Wish Pool.

Obtaining either of the two will give you access to all chapters for the new Myth that’s also available as part of this event: Yin Yang Sundering. You can read all the lore once either of the two Memories have been unlocked, and you won’t even need to upgrade either of them.

The Lost Souls event has also kicked off alongside the new update. You can take part to claim a 4-Star Solar Slor Memory Pair for Caleb: Duskshard Dreams and Duskshard Lotus. You can also earn the 3-Star Memory, Lotus Bond, alongside some other freebies like more Wishes, Diamonds, Photo Poses, and an event-exclusive title.

After you unlock Caleb’s Netherlord Companion, you may want to fight alongside him to get another 4-Star Memory for free. You’ll need to challenge the the Rehearsal Stage to do so, and your first clear is guaranteed to get you the Duskshard Lotus Memory.

If you’re new to Love and Deepspace, or you simply want a refresher, we’ve put together a guide to help you wrap your head around Myths; how they work and how to unlock them. Banners are also an important part of any gacha game, Love and Deepspace included, so here’s how banners work, and what the current and next banners are.

#4039. Base PS5's QSSR Enhancer Coming to 6 More Games, in Spider-Man 2 Now

Control Resonant, Arc Raiders, and more upgraded

Sony has announced it is expanding support for its QSSR graphics enhancer on base PS5 to six more PS5 games in the coming weeks.

Through a free update, the feature is live right now in Marvel's Spider-Man 2. In addition, the following titles will receive support for QSSR soon:

More games will receive QSSR support in the future too, as Sony continues to work with developers in implementing the visual enhancement technology. "Developers are just getting started," Sony states. with the PS5 Pro has had PSSR since launch, which was recently upgraded via new version, the QSSR tech is designed for the base PS5 system.

Ghost of Yotei and Marvel's Wolverine also support the feature.

News Sony Confirms Refined Version of Acclaimed PSSR Upscaler for Base PS5, with 'Remarkable' Potential

"It's great to be improving the PS5 this far into the generation"

QSSR support in Marvel's Spider-Man 2 is live now, and head of technology at Insomniac Games, Mike Fitzgerald, told the PlayStation Blog you should spot improved image stability and sharpness across both the Fidelity and Performance modes in the game.

Remedy expects to have QSSR support added to Control Resonant in December, at which point the PS5 title will have a "more stable and detailed image". Here's a comparison video:

Embark Studios is supporting QSSR across both its multiplayer games, The Finals and Arc Raiders. Once the PS5 patch is applied, expect "increased sharpness, better environmental clarity and overall visual improvements". Here is another comparison video for Arc Raiders specifically:

When No Man's Sky is updated with QSSR support, it'll "render the universe in sharper, cleaner and more beautiful detail, while delivering the best possible framerate". The patch should become available in the next few weeks.

#4038. Rimworld-inspired colony sim Stardeus gets a huge update representing a year's worth of expansion and revision, with new tools for evil AI overlords

"Stardeus is in an early stage in terms of bulk and complexity, but it's already a pleasant blend of interesting ideas that generate a mostly relaxing vibe," wrote gallant star captain.exe Sin Vega in our 2022 analysis of Rimworld-influenced colony manager Stardeus. "One to watch for sure." Well, let it not be said that we weren't watching.

Stardeus has received a gargantuan early access update that has been "a year in the making," according to developer Kodo Linija. It's still a game about being an AI running a badly damaged interstellar colony ship in top-down view – sending drones to restore the damage, before waking the quarrelsome human popsicles from their slumber. But the new version introduces a quest system and a new opening tutorial chain, the ability to form alliances with other starfaring factions, the possibility of lifelong injury due to failed surgery, and the timely option to become an evil AI and mind-control your crew with beta waves, amongst other dastardly antics.

It introduces a new interface and a new ship aesthetic, a trust system that governs the odds of a mutiny, and a revised colonist skill system. There's also a freshened-up ground combat element that's now built around "cover, suppression, stuns and fleeing", and a new approach to space battles that's all about managing Flux generated when you fire weapons or take shield damage. The update notes on Steam tote more than 1,500 changes, with the dev enthusing that there is "hardly a system in the game that wasn't rebuilt, reworked or expanded".

I confess, I hadn't heard of Stardeus before. It sounds like fun, in the Dwarf Fortressian sense. The 1.0 rollout is due in "approximately Q1 2027".

#4037. The Petit Planet beta is coming back with new updates, but you still need to hope for an invite

If you've been missing Petit Planet since it was last available to play, you'll be happy to know that HoYoverse is hosting another test soon.

It’s been quite a while since we’ve heard anything about Petit Planet, the upcoming game from Genshin Impact and Honkai: Star Rail developer HoYoverse. By most accounts, Petit Planet is the studio’s take on Animal Crossing, though with a few interesting ideas of its own.

The game’s most recent test took place all the way back in November, but its next big test isn’t far off.

HoYoverse announced today that Petit Planet’s Stardrift Test is scheduled for April 21. This latest build will be available on PC, Android, and iOS. The beta will include new Neighbors, an updated Starsea Voyage, and more for you to do at the Galactic Bazaar.

Seeing as interacting with Neighbors is a core part of this life sim RPG, the confirmation that new faces will be available in this test is big news. Each Neighbor in Petit Planet is a character, with their own personalty and life story.

The Starsea Voyage now includes a map, too, which you can use to take you to other Islets. If you played any of the previous tests, you should already be familiar with this feature.

The only bit of bad news here is that this remains a closed beta. You’re still encouraged to sign up on the official website, but you’re not guaranteed access. HoYoverse said that only a portion of players who sign up will be invited to the upcoming beta.

Petit Planet remains without a release date. If nothing else, it’ll be interesting to see the progress the game has made since last November’s beta.

#4036. Review: CRKD Ult Pro Controller For Switch 1 & 2 - A Decent Pad Let Down By Awful Shoulder & Bumper Buttons

CRKD is the latest accessory manufacturer to produce a premium alternative to Nintendo’s own Pro Controller on Switch 2, but it’s one that needs a lot of refinement if it’s to become a legitimate competitor.

Priced at $69.99 / €79.99 / £64.99, the Ult Pro sits below the Pro Controller and roughly at par with Gulikit’s excellent TT line, price-wise. It comes feature-packed with TMR (Tunnel Magnetoresistance) analogue sticks, Hall Effect triggers, four back buttons, two extra bumper inputs, four profile modes, adjustable rumble, a charging stand, and more.

The analogue sticks feel good, featuring a more convex shape that you don’t often see these days. There’s a thin ridge near the edge of the grip which helps keep you aware of where your thumbs are sitting. It’s also worth mentioning that the grips can be removed for replacement designs, but these are sold separately – it would have been nice if at least one alternative were included in the box as standard. Otherwise, the TMR technology should keep stick-drift at bay.

The default D-pad design (again, you can swap it out if you want) is circular with a raised cross representing the four cardinal directions. I like this a lot: it feels quiet yet retains accuracy during gameplay, and I found it reliable for platformers like Super Mario World and action games like Contra.

The ABXY buttons unfortunately aren’t mechanical with a satisfying click, but they do the job well enough. Like the analogue sticks, they’re slightly convex in design and are spaced at just the right distance to allow easy, intuitive access to all of them. I also like the colours; CRKD avoided the exact same colour scheme as both the SNES and Xbox 360 pads, but it’s got the same vibe (you can also opt for an all-black controller, if you wish).

The shoulder and bumper buttons, sadly, let the side down. You can adjust the shoulder button travel distance, opting between a short, clicky input or a full, smooth trigger input. To be clear, the Switch 2 doesn’t support analogue triggers for anything except the Nintendo Switch Online GameCube pad, so your choice here is purely down to personal preference.

While the full-motion trigger feels pretty good, the clicky, tactile option is horrible. Rather than offering a satisfying click, they instead feel weak and spongy, almost as if the slightest bit of force will snap (or ‘CRK’, amirite) whatever mechanism is inside to produce the clicky response. I hated this, and CRKD should address it promptly for any future revisions.

As for the bumper inputs, the additional ‘L2’ and ‘R2’ inputs are far too close to the main ‘L1’ and ‘R1’ buttons on either side. So essentially, when resting your index finger across the bumpers, you’re covering both the standard button and the extra input, making it far too easy to accidentally press the wrong button. CRKD would have been wise to space these further apart and make the main bumpers larger (8BitDo’s Pro 3 is a good reference point), or just remove the extra inputs entirely.

Speaking of extra inputs, the four additional buttons on the rear are perfectly fine – I’ve got no major issues with these, and they’ll no doubt prove useful for anyone looking to gain the upper hand in Modern Warfare 4 (or perhaps even sprint while moving the camera in Ocarina of Time). The only downside is that they produce quite a loud click when pressed, though I think this is down to the plastic used for the exterior casing – it feels a tad cheap for the price.

You can map any input to the additional buttons — the four on the back and the two on top — by using the ‘P’ (Program) button underneath the D-pad. You also have four profiles if you want to swap between configurations. CRKD neglected to include decent instructions with the product, and the QR code for an online manual led me to a dead page, but it does at least have a video on YouTube if you need help remapping buttons and setting up profiles.

With the function buttons (i.e. Start, Select, Capture), CRKD bizarrely opted for two rocking inputs. With the left one, for example, you push it up for Select and down for Capture. It’s so weird – it works, but it’s weird. There’s no dedicated ‘C’ button; instead, there's an integrated macro to navigate to the Chat app if you push down on the right rocker.

You can connect the Ult Pro to your console via three different methods. Bluetooth is standard and works exactly how you’d expect: just hold down the large, black button until it flashes blue to enter pairing mode. You also have a USB dongle stored inside the charging dock, so plug this into your Switch 2 dock and you can pair that way instead. Finally, you can simply connect it via a USB-A to USB-C cable. The difference between these is, for me at least, not noticeable, but if you’re someone who’s particularly sensitive to lag, you might have a clear preference here.

Oh, and there’s no wake-up support for Switch 2. Sorry.

Finally, the Ult Pro lasts for around 15 hours on a single charge, and if you use the included charging dock, you’ll likely never need to worry about it dying on you. The dock design is simple and looks neat next to the TV when charging. You can also replace the rechargeable battery in the controller itself if need be, or simply use a pair of AA batteries.

There’s a lot to like about the Ult Pro, including its TMR sticks, the D-pad, the charging dock, and the lovely coloured ABXY inputs. Unfortunately, CRKD really dropped the ball with the shoulder and bumper buttons – I hate them, and they really ruin the whole thing for me.

With no wake-up support and a fairly cheap-feeling exterior case, this isn’t quite the Pro Controller competitor I was hoping for, but with some tweaks and refinements, I think the company could be onto something. Do I actually like those rocking function buttons, though? Honestly, I’m still not sure.

The sample used in this review was provided by CRKD.

#4035. Xbox Playback Is Now Available, Take A Look Back At Your Xbox History

"Your games. Your milestones. Your story."

One of my favourite things to do is look back at the Xbox games I've been playing, the achievements I've unlocked, and all of my cool unique stats that make me the Xbox gamer I am.

This year, Xbox is doing something a bit different. Unlike previous Xbox 'Year in Review' roundups, which cover the past 11 or 12 months, Xbox Playback takes things all the way back to the beginning, celebrating your story through Xbox's 25 years.

You can access your own Xbox Playback from the official Xbox site, where you'll need to sign in with your Microsoft account. There's this whole song-and-dance animation, sorta like Spotify's Wrapped, which takes you through stuff like the first game you played, what year you played the most, what % of most played time across all of Xbox, achievements, and loads of other really cool stuff. Then, you can share it to social media if you fancy.

As you can see above, Xbox CTO Scott Van Vliet created his account in 2006, has earned 28,528 gamerscore, and has 4,375 hours played: which is only in the top 4.8% of hours played, whereas yours truly is in the 0.2%. What can I say? I guess I'm an Xbox gamer after all.

Another thing that's really cool about Xbox Playback is that, for the first time ever, players will be able to access and view it directly from their console. No browser required. According to Xbox, it should appear soon, so keep an eye out!

We're keen to find out what your Xbox Playback says about your journey with Xbox through the years, so please do let us know what that looks like down in the comments. What percentage of hours played are you? What was your first game? When did you join? Let us hear it!

#4034. Oblivion and Skyrim’s gap was bridged by forward-looking books about a murderous floating island, so why is The Elder Scrolls 6 stuck reanimating a world that’s stood still since 2011

Why the Umbri-hell has time stopped in Tamriel?

Long waits between mainline entries in a series aren’t a new phenomenon, if perhaps a bit more common nowadays due to big games' ballooning development cycles. It took about 23 years for BioWare’s Baldur's Gate 2 to be followed up by Larian’s Baldur’s Gate 3, though there were a decent amount of spin-offs and remasters peppered between the two.

The wait for The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel hasn’t stretched on that long quite yet, but as Bethesda finally revealed concrete details about it just in time for Skyrim's 15th birthday, it really hit home for me that TES VI will be tasked with restoring motion to a world where calendars have been stuck in the 201st year of the 4th era since 2011. Perhaps it’s because I’m still in my twenties and haven’t lived long enough to see that many things I like pause their forward march for this long before returning. There’s also a good chance my expectations of timelines rolling forward on a regular basis without the need for a whole new entry are coloured by the constant stream of new stuff fed into most games via updates and live service passes these days.

However, when I look back at the interregnum between the last two Elder Scrolls games, Oblivion and Skyrim, I can’t help but feel that what Bethesda and ZeniMax have packed into the gap between Skyrim and Sentinel might have done the latter no favours. Sure, The Elder Scrolls Online has arguably meant that there’s been far more for series fans to sink their teeth into between mainline games than ever before, but because the MMO's a prequel, none of its tales and lore push the Elder Scrolls' timeline forwards. Meanwhile mobile and card game spin-offs like The Elder Scrolls: Blades, The Elder Scrolls: Legends, and The Elder Scrolls: Castles have all either slotted in before Skyrim or not been tied to a specific point in time.

On one hand, that leaves the devs a nice clean slate to take the sixth entry wherever they like narratively upon the conclusion of the Dragonborn’s adventures. On the other, Bethesda has missed the opportunity to paint out the world and further set up the stakes for Sentinel in the interim. Back when we were waiting for Skyrim's original release, the developers were pumping out spin-off books that daubed some fresh adventures onto the Elder Scrolls' canvas.

I bought these books - 2009’s The Infernal City and 2011’s Lord of Souls - ages ago upon hearing their tales referenced in the sorts of Elder Scrolls lore videos which appeal to sad nerds of my ilk, but have only gotten around to reading past the opening chapters in recent months.

In hindsight, I think I bounced off them that first time because it just felt a bit weird to be reading about set characters getting up to adventures in Tamriel rather than setting off on them in the boots of my own custom created protagonist. I didn’t run into the same with The Witcher, as you’re seeing that world through Gerry from the River’s eyes no matter where you turn. Anyway, the two Elder Scrolls novels by American author Greg Keyes tell the tale of the Umbriel crisis which took place 48 years after the Oblivion crisis and about 153 years before Skyrim’s dragon crisis (Tamriel does love a crisis). The Umbriel crisis saw a floating island powered by souls and formed via some Daedric drama, carve a path of destruction from Black Marsh to the Imperial City. Yep, the empire’s not-Roman soldiers had to fight a flying hunk of land. At one point some mages had to float a legion up in the sky so they could get their bottoms kicked by Umbriel’s defenders.

As you might’ve gathered, the books take the opportunity to tell a story which - especially in terms of where tech was in 2009 - wouldn’t necessarily fit an Elder Scrolls game. Or, at least, not one of the more straight-laced variety Bethesda have made in their post-Morrowind days. A lot of time’s spent looking through the eyes of two characters who’ve snuck aboard Umbriel, the floating island, after it destroyed their hometown and have to adjust to the strange customs of its inhabitant lords and their underlings before finding ways to help take it down. On the ground, things take a more familiar form, as a very serious Dark Elf named Sul and a nepo baby Imperial prince trek across bits of Cyrodiil, Morrowind, and Elsweyr on a quest to do their bit in vanquishing the threat. Then, there’s a Penitus Oculatus spy named Colin trying to figure out if the Umbriel Crisis is an inside job of some sort and a few tales of regular Imperial troops working to evacuate citizens living in the floating island’s path. In an Elder Scrolls game, you’d get some of that, but not be able to hop from person to person chapter by chapter in the fashion the books do.

Umbriel slowly floats across Black Marsh, southern Morrowind and Cyrodiil with an army of zombies in tow, much like this article’s about to float into mildly spoilery territory for the two books. You see, The Infernal City and Lord of Souls outline what happened to cause the red year, a volcanic eruption which took the land of the Dark Elves from the beautifully alien place it was at the time of The Elder Scrolls 3 and reduced it to the ash-covered wasteland it’s outlined to be at the time of Skyrim. As the latter game’s lore books would subsequently set in stone, Baar Dau - the meteor suspended in the air above Vivec City at the time of Morrowind - fell and destroyed the city following the disappearance of the metropolis’ namesake ex-Tribunal god-king. The books reveal that the big rock didn’t fall the moment Vivec vanished, but was kept afloat by a device called the Ingenium, which is essentially a magic box powered by regular soul sacrifices. Two Dunmer, Vuhon and the aforementioned Sul, ended up having a fight rooted in the tech’s murderous nature and that’s actually what led Baar Dau to finally hit the ground.

Either way, the meteor falls, but that's not an insubstantial bit of backstory for a source outside of the games to add to the Elder Scrolls’ canon. Also wound into the tale of how Umbriel came to be is a bunch of extra flesh on the bone of the relationship between Daedric prince Clavicus Vile and Umbra. In the games, the latter’s always just been a powerful sword which imprints a new personality onto its wielder, but in the books it’s portrayed as a being capable of nicking some of Vile’s godly power and plotting to escape the prince’s realm of Oblivion via the building of Umbriel. Beyond those, the books also offer a chance to get to know emperor Titus Mede I, the warlord who took over the Empire following a post-Oblivion crisis interregnum and whose offspring you murder during Skyrim’s Dark Brotherhood questline.

None of this is anything close to required knowledge for playing Skyrim. No characters from the books pop up to say hello, likely because enough time’s passed for most to perish of natural causes. The sole reference I can recall comes via a chat about a location called Sleeping Tree Camp, which isn’t tied to any of the main questlines. You can, and I did for a long time, totally ignore these time-bridging tomes. That said, I do feel that having now taken the time to read them has helped me see the history of Tamriel as something not as strictly limited to the specific snapshots in time presented by each of the games.

Tales like these, which aren’t conveyed with as much natural emotional detachment as I tend to feel when reading much-condensed accounts of historical events or far off places on the pages of in-game lore books, really help in creating the illusion that The Elder Scrolls’ world is growing and evolving as our own does. It’s not just a snow globe that only shifts whenever some prophesied hero piloted by a controller or keyboard rocks up to shake it.

I do think, in large part due to the size of the real world gap between it and Skyrim, The Elder Scrolls 6 would have and still could benefit from having spin-offs like these to keep gently nudging the timeline forwards. A complicating factor is that judging by this week’s teaser, Sentinel seems like it could be set in the 206th year of the fourth era, a mere five years after the events of Skyrim. That’d mean no 200-ish years of wiggle room in which to slot some spin-off stories without serious risk of influencing things that’d have to be reflected in the new game. Unless Bethesda wanted to either put serious barriers up around where the spin-off could tread or get into a game of arbitrarily deciding what is or isn’t canon. With some collaboration, it could certainly be done, but it could also be a headache the studio wouldn’t want.

It’s likely too late to start the ball rolling now anyway, but that doesn’t stop it being worth asking why Bethesda and their famously adaptation-loving corporate bosses at Microsoft didn’t make sure they had something akin to these books in the works when Sentinel was punted down the road in favour of Starfield.

You did this well once, why haven’t you managed to pull it off again this time? I’m hoping that isn’t the inquiry which’ll come to define The Elder Scrolls 6 as much as questions about where a chunk of the old Bethesda magic had gone did with the studio’s trip to space. Lest the next long wait for a game from them be packed with even more uncomfortable silence.

#4033. Heartopia celebrates 30 million downloads with new outfits, permanent price cuts

Heartopia's rise has continued since its launch earlier this year, and the game's developer isn't slowing down with updates.

Heartopia has kicked off a new event to celebrate passing 30 million downloads. Just a couple of weeks after delivering the vintage Hollywood-themed Dreamlight Cinematics event, developer XD Games has revealed The Whimsical Tea Party, a limited-time Gilded Acorn Exhibition.

The event kicked off on Saturday, bringing some new themed content to the game.

Whimsical Tea Party’s biggest addition are the new outfits, including the Wandering Traveler, and the Duke Bunny outfits. Each outfit is available in three different colours. Another thing Heartopia events bring are building materials sets.

This one adds the Labyrinth furniture building materials set, the Hedgehog & Flamingo mallet, and the Cheshire Cat pet costume. Speaking of outfits, XD Games is dropping the in-game prices for a number of items permanently.

All original pet outfits now cost 66.7% less. Those of the Common variety will now cost 10 Souvenir Ticket Stubs, instead of the previous 30. Rare pet outfits will cost 5 Souvenir Ticket Stubs, down from 15.

If you happened to buy Common or Rare original pet outfits between July 17, 2024 and March 22, 2026, you’ll be refunded the difference. This will automatically show up in-game the next time you log in. If you instead purchased those pet outfits between March 23 and April 4, you should look forward to your refund before April 10.

Keeping with the theme of freebies, Heartopia is also celebrating surpassing 30 million downloads worldwide by giving all players a small gift package in-game. This freebie is available until May 29, so you should have enough time to claim it.

For comprehensive guidance on where to find birds, bugs, and fish, check out our Heartopia bird locations, Heartopia bug locations, and Heartopia fish locations guides. #4032. "Arkane is profitable," say Marvel's Blade developers in fiery new statement, "just not profitable enough for Microsoft"

Unionised workers reiterate call for a "solid offer" for Arkane Lyon's future

Unionised workers at Dishonored developers Arkane Lyon have published a fresh statement about the progress of negotiations with Microsoft over the studio's potential closure. Aside from calling on Xbox management to make a redundancy offer proportionate to Microsoft's colossal market value, they accuse the parent company of creating the very economic conditions cited as a reason for closing Arkane, and thereby "sabotaging" development of the forthcoming Marvel's Blade.

Published by French union Le Syndicat des Travailleureuses du Jeu Vidéo - one of two unions who represent workers at Arkane, the other being Printemps écologique, who didn't issue a similar message - the official English translation of the statement begins by insisting that "work on Blade is going fine". It maintains that the game will measure up to previous Arkane Lyon releases, despite the stress of trying to pin down a new owner for the company, after Microsoft announced plans to part ways with Arkane and several other studios back in July. The writers then take Microsoft to task for making an "outrageously low" redundancy offer to Arkane's workers, and further accuse the Xbox company of essentially setting Arkane up to fail by imposing a hiring freeze and depriving the studio of resources.

"Microsoft chose to justify the closure on economic reasons," the workers write. "But Microsoft is actually why those economic reasons even exist." It asserts that Microsoft froze hiring "for 19 months, which artificially caused delay and additional cost", only to then use those delays and extra costs "as a reason to close down the studio". It also claims that Microsoft have "systematically" deprived Arkane of cash, by means of corporate mechanisms the statement doesn't make wholly clear. "Even this closure itself is done against any financial logic, as closing Arkane today would probably be more expensive than finishing the game," the statement adds, without going into detail.

"The truth is that Microsoft based its decision only on stone cold and inhuman logic, in which our lives, projects and dreams are voided, so we can better serve Microsoft’s short term financial goals," the workers continue. They accuse Microsoft of "the brutal application of a never-ending search for maximum profit optimization", citing years of mass layoffs across the Xbox company together with the recent voluntary buyout offering. "Arkane is profitable," they add. "Just not profitable enough for Microsoft."

The workers want a "solid offer" from Microsoft regarding the studio's post-Xbox future, declaring that "when the company who decided that Arkane has to shut down is, according to many sources the most profitable in the world, with a net profit of more than 133 Billions of dollars in the past years, it would be the bare minimum to ensure that the redundancy plan offered by Microsoft is on [par] with their means."

If Arkane have to close, the unionised workers call on Microsoft "to release funds commensurate with Microsoft’s status as a corporation, to make sure that the workers are compensated in line with the loss suffered". They'd like a redundancy payment of €200,000, two years of "redeployment support", a package of "shared resources for training and studio creation", including a residual bonus, and "compensation up to the redundancy payment for independent workers’ contract breach", to safeguard the livelihoods of freelancers and contractors.

The warring parties at Xbox and Arkane have until 11th December this year to figure out a deal. Reportedly, Ubisoft are among those looking to buy Arkane - a source of some concern, given that Ubisoft have also recently closed a number of studios and laid many people off. I'm not sure I'd be waving my wallet around if I were using my other hand to sign pink slips.

#4031. Honkai: Star Rail players are eating good, with Version 4.2 and third anniversary celebrations kicking off later this month

Honkai: Star Rail will be celebrating its third anniversary just days after it delivers a major update, and there's quite a bit to chew on in this one.

HoYoverse just wrapped up a stacked Honkai: Star Rail Special Program, delivering the one-two punch of revealing the game’s next major update, and detailing what you can expect from its third anniversary celebrations.

First off, Version 4.2, dubbed So Laughed the Masses, arrives April 22, making two characters playable, and bringing back a host of beloved characters for re-runs. The new update continues the Phantasmoon Games arc, as the story takes an especially suspect new development.

The big inciting incident of this new chapter is the reveal that whoever wins the Phantasmoon Games will also become the permanent Aeon of Elation. Meanwhile, Fulwish has invited all Supplicants to the Fulwish TV HQ to announce their intention to host a TV debate about the ultimate goal of the Phantasmoon Games.

Naturally, you’re invited, and you’ll have to overcome the challenges that await to gather more Wishpower.

Our first new arrival is Silver Wolf LV.999, with whom you should already be familiar from her Version 1 form. The difference now, of course, is that she’s getting a brand-new alternate kit, since — true to her new name — she's evolved into a Godmode Player upon reaching Level 999. Silver Wolf LV.999 is a 5-Star Imaginary character on the Path of Elation.

Her main combat trick is the ability to rack up Hidden MMR, which is what allows her to eventually activate her Cartridge and settle into the aforementioned Godmode state. While in that form, she shifts the entire battle into the virtual world, pulling in both teams into her gaming domain.

This is essentially a world under her control, which is why she can unlock a Reward Stage at the start of her turn, which lets her spawn in-game items. When picked up, these items can turn the tide of battle.

Keeping up with the ultra-gamer persona, Silver Wolf's Aha Instant strike blasts all enemies with a laser cannon, dealing massive damage. Perhaps her most interesting ability is being able to hack into the battlefield when she’s not actively on the team, something she can do when a teammate falls under enemy control.

Evanescia is the other newly-playable character, who has thus far only been an observer of the Phantasmoon Games, as well as one of the most prominent new characters we've met so far on Planarcadia. V4.2 sees the girl join the roster as a 5-Star Physical character who’s likewise on the Path of Elation. As she fights, she always accumulates Certified Banger, when she earns the title she’s able to simultaneously regenerate Energy and maintain her damage.

Evanescia’s damage continues to increase the more Certified Banger she accumulates, triggering an attack from Master Fox upon reaching a certain threshold, which deals damage to all enemies and regenerates Energy for herself. Her Elation Skill adds a bit of a performance to her kit, and is capable of hitting all enemies.

You may have noticed the Path of Elation theme in this one, so you won’t be surprised to learn that the Elation Trailblazer variant on the main playable character is also joining the team in 4.2. There’s a new weapon that starts off as a glow stick but can transform into a lightblade as you deal damage, and, yes, gain Certified Banger.

It can also turn into nunchucks, which delivers a unique flurry of attacks on all enemies surrounding the character, dealing multiple instances of damage. You can also use it to cheer for a teammate, hyping them up.

Version 4.2 Warp Events will bring back six characters. The first half will see reruns of The Dahlia, Castorice, and Firefly. The second half will give you another shot at unlocking Tribbie, Sunday, and Feixiao. What’s more, four of the game’s characters will be buffed in this update, so you may want to reconsider putting them them back on your team. They are Firefly, Huohuo, Seele, and Welt.

As part of the same update, you can expect the debut of the Cosmic Data Roaming event, which goes live alongside the anniversary celebrations. The event lets you live the life of a streamer.

Currency Wars is getting a big expansion, too. Likewise, the Cosmicon Collective is getting its version 2.0 update, adding new decks, dice as well as a new team challenge game mode.

As for the big third anniversary celebration, it will kick off in-game on April 26, bringing back Festive Gifts. The event will only be available during these celebrations, and it will once again be gifting players who log in regularly a total of 20 pulls.

You’ll also be able to a select a blessing card from a companion of your choice to receive a special gift of 1,600 Stellar Jades. The same celebrations will also seeHuohuo and Robin permanently added to the Stellar Convergence store. You’ll have another chance to exchange a Golden Companion Spirit for any companion you like in that store, too — and all you need to do is log in anytime between Versions 4.2 and 4.4. This being a new year for Honkai: Star Rail, the top-up double bonus is resetting, meaning anyone who tops up their wallet will get a hefty bonus.

Elsewhere, you’ll find new items in the Gift of Stardust Store, including a new outfit for Castorice. Between the time 4.2 launches and when the celebrations begin, you’ll be able to try your luck in Aha's Chosen: Spreading Elation Everywhere, an online event where you can leave a message for a chance to win various prizes.

#4030. "BioWare's closure represents an immense loss to and possibly a targeted attack on Canada's cultural legacy" argues petition calling on Canadian government to step in

1,662 Canadians have been verified as signing it thus far

Calls for the Canadian government to help ressurect recently shuttered RPG makers BioWare have progressed from a single post by a politician to a petition with enough signatures that it looks set to be presented to the Canadian House of Commons for an official response. So far, 1,662 people from the country of maple syrup and also other things have signed this call for their leaders to consider stepping in.

"BioWare is one of Canada's most important cultural exports to the world in the 21st century, selling tens of millions of units of their video games globally," declares the petition, started by Brendan Routh and authorised by Vancouver Kingsway MP Don Davies.

"BioWare's productions champion the values of inclusivity, tolerance, democracy, justice, and civil rights that are at the centre of Canada's national identity," its run of bullet points continues. "BioWare has been shuttered by its American parent company Electronic Arts, now owned by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund and Jared Kushner's Affinity Partners and BioWare's closure represents an immense loss to and possibly a targeted attack on Canada's cultural legacy."

With all of that in mind, the petition calls on the Canadian Government to "provide BioWare with the capital necessary to secure independence of themselves and their intellectual property from Electronic Arts and resume business as an independent, Canadian company". The Canadians who've signed also want their leaders to "protect Canadian businesses and cultural institutions from being dictated by American and foreign corporate interests" and "champion the values of inclusivity, tolerance, democracy, justice, and civil rights at the centre of Canada's national identity by preserving BioWare's invaluable contribution to the global entertainment industry".

Thus far, the petition's amassed 1,662 verified signatures from citizens across Canada, putting it above the 500 verified signature threshold required for it to be presented to the country's House of Commons. That'll be followed by the tabling of an official response from the Canadian government.

As with some of the responses from political bodies the likes of the Stop Killing Games campaign have gotten over the years, I find it hard not to see this petition not being greeted with an answer along the lines of 'We do care about this and thank you for raising it, but we're not really gonna do much here'. I think a full BioWare resurrection with government backing is highly unlikely, but finding some way to enshrine the studio's legacy or contribution to Canada's games industry and arts culture seems a lot more easily doable.

A big statue of Blokeshep and Femshep surrounded by their crew of potential allies somewhere in Edmonton, maybe. Or a big stone middle finger that's always required to be aimed at a poster for the next Star Wars film/game/TV show/bit of merch.
